title: About
text:
Hi, I’m Wantida (Wow)
I’m a veterinary epidemiologist and disease ecologist working at the overlap of veterinary medicine, wildlife health, and One Health. I try to keep one foot in the field — with animals, landscapes, and communities — and one foot in the data.
Right now I’m a postdoctoral researcher at Penn State (Department of Ecosystem Science and Management), where I work on targeted surveillance for SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer across Pennsylvania and eight other U.S. states, in collaboration with USDA and USGS. My days involve R, GPS movement data, contact networks, and many, many deer.
Before Penn State, my PhD at Massey University (New Zealand) focused on wild bovid habitat and infectious disease risk in Thailand — using habitat suitability models and disease-dynamic simulations to map where threatened wild cattle species (gaur, banteng, wild water buffalo) overlap with domestic livestock and shared pathogens.

title: About
text:
What I care about

One Health thinking — treating human, animal, and environmental health as one connected system.
Wildlife conservation — especially threatened species and the landscapes they depend on.
Disease ecology — understanding where and why pathogens emerge, not just what they are.
Open, reproducible science — sharing code and data so other researchers (and future me) can build on the work.

title: Wantida Horpiencharoen
text:
Wantida Horpiencharoen
  Veterinary epidemiologist · Wildlife disease ecologist · One Health researcher

Hi — I’m Wow, a postdoctoral researcher at Penn State working on SARS-CoV-2 surveillance in white-tailed deer. I’m a veterinarian (DVM, Kasetsart) and disease ecologist (PhD, Massey University) whose work sits at the wildlife–livestock–human interface.
My research combines GPS movement analysis, contact networks, species distribution modelling, and stochastic compartmental models to understand how pathogens circulate in wildlife — and what that means for conservation and public health.
I care about One Health thinking, open reproducible science in R, and fieldwork that stays close to the animals and communities it’s meant to serve.

title: Research
text:
My research explores how pathogens move among wildlife, livestock, and people — and how that knowledge can guide conservation and public health decisions. I work at three overlapping scales: the pathogen, the host community, and the landscape.
Below are the main stories that tie my work together. Each section links to the paper. Figures from my Royal Society and Wiley papers are reproduced under their original CC-BY licences; the mastitis diagram is an original schematic I drew to summarise the 2019 Preventive Veterinary Medicine paper.

title: Research
section: SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer — current postdoctoral work
text:
SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer — current postdoctoral work
At Penn State I’m analysing GPS movement data and contact networks from white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) across Pennsylvania and eight other U.S. states, in collaboration with USDA and USGS. The question: can deer act as a reservoir for SARS-CoV-2, and if so, what does that mean for spillback into people?
I combine step-selection and home-range analysis (using the amt package in R), contact-network construction, stochastic compartmental models, and Bayesian inference of transmission parameters. A first paper on the Pennsylvania contact network is in preparation.

title: Research
section: Wild bovids, habitat, and infectious disease in Southeast Asia — my PhD
text:
Wild bovids, habitat, and infectious disease in Southeast Asia — my PhD
My doctoral work at Massey University asked a simple question with surprisingly complex answers: where do Thailand’s threatened wild bovids still have suitable habitat, and where does that habitat overlap with domestic cattle — creating places of shared pathogens?
Five bovid species still roam Thailand: gaur (Bos gaurus), banteng (Bos javanicus), wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee), mainland serow (Capricornis sumatraensis) and Chinese goral (Naemorhedus griseus). Their populations have declined sharply under habitat fragmentation, hunting, and contact with domestic livestock that share their grazing grounds and pathogens.

Mapping the habitat that remains
In Horpiencharoen et al. (Royal Society Open Science, 2024), I built ecological niche models for all five species across 13 Asian countries and showed that over half of the suitable habitat for these wild bovids lies outside protected areas — meaning that conservation has to happen on the working landscape, not just inside reserves.



Habitat suitability across the five wild bovid species of Southeast Asia, from Horpiencharoen et al. (2024). Warmer colours indicate higher predicted habitat suitability. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY (R. Soc. Open Sci. 11, 240574).




Layering species together — where the landscape holds many at once
Suitability for one species is useful. Suitability for several species stacked together is what matters for designing conservation corridors. Summing the per-species maps gives a habitat-richness surface that flags the places where the most wild bovids could coexist — and where protection and monitoring give the biggest return.



Habitat-richness map derived by stacking the five species-specific suitability layers. Darker pixels are places predicted to be suitable for more wild bovid species at once — the highest-priority corridors for multi-species conservation. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY.


Read the paper → DOI 10.1098/rsos.240574


Where wildlife and livestock collide: mapping pathogen-transmission risk
In Horpiencharoen et al. (Conservation Science and Practice, 2025), I overlaid those habitat-suitability maps with cattle density to find the interface zones — landscapes where wild bovids and domestic cattle are most likely to share pathogens.
The interface is dominated by forest edges, cropland, and unclassified forest, and — strikingly — Kuiburi National Park alone holds 274 km² of high-risk area for gaur and banteng. For wild water buffalo the largest risk zone (126 km²) overlaps with Huai Thabthan–Had Samran. These maps give conservation managers and veterinary services specific, mappable places to focus surveillance and mitigation.



Figure 1 from Horpiencharoen et al. (2025) — Bivariate maps of wild bovid habitat suitability (blue) against cattle density (yellow); dark red pixels are the high-risk interface. © 2025 The Authors, CC-BY (Conservation Science and Practice, e70111).


Read the paper → DOI 10.1111/csp2.70111


What happens if disease actually crosses the fence?
A map tells you where pathogens could spill, but not what that would do to the population. In Horpiencharoen et al. (Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 2024), I built stochastic compartmental models of a gaur population under six cattle-borne diseases: anthrax, bovine tuberculosis, haemorrhagic septicaemia, lumpy skin disease, foot-and-mouth disease, and brucellosis.
The key findings:

Chronic infections (brucellosis, bTB) cause the greatest long-term damage. Frequency-dependent brucellosis drove gaur populations down by ~97 %, with extinction in 16 % of simulations.
Acute, high-fatality diseases (anthrax) had surprisingly small effects — infected animals die quickly and “burn out” the outbreak.
Disease-free populations grew by an average of 228 % over 100 years — so healthy gaur can recover, if given the chance.




Modelled gaur population dynamics over 100 years, with and without each disease. Left column: single example stochastic simulations. Right column: 100 stochastic simulations. Compartments shown are susceptible (S), exposed (E), infected (I), recovered/immune (R) and removed (M), plus total. From Horpiencharoen et al. (2024), © The Authors, CC-BY (J. R. Soc. Interface 21, 20240278).


The total-population view at the end of 100 years makes the ordering of threats unmistakeable: the chronic, density-dependent infections (brucellosis, bovine tuberculosis) hollow the population out over decades, while the acute high-fatality infections burn through quickly and rebound. Disease-free populations grow steadily — a reminder that healthy gaur recover when given the chance.



Projected gaur population sizes after 100 years under each disease scenario, relative to the disease-free baseline. The separation between chronic and acute disease effects is stark — brucellosis and bTB dominate the long-term risk picture. © 2024 The Authors, CC-BY.


Read the paper → DOI 10.1098/rsif.2024.0278

title: Research
section: Dairy cows & mastitis — finding the risk factors that matter
text:
Dairy cows & mastitis — finding the risk factors that matter
Before wild bovids, my MSc and early veterinary work focused on a very different interface: small-holder dairy farms in western Thailand. Clinical mastitis is a costly, chronic problem for these farmers, and ordinary regression often hides the relationships between farm practices, pathogens, and treatment outcomes.


Sampling locations of 43 smallholder dairy farms across three central-western provinces — Kanchanaburi, Ratchaburi, and Nakhon Pathom — with the sampled districts shaded on the inset. From Horpiencharoen et al. (2019), Preventive Veterinary Medicine 164, 49–55 (DOI).

In Horpiencharoen et al. (Preventive Veterinary Medicine, 2019), my co-authors and I sampled 100 quarters of milk from 100 cows across 43 dairies and built a Bayesian network that connects farm management (floor type, dry-cow therapy, milking-machine hygiene, parity) to the pathogens isolated in mastitis milk (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, E. coli, S. dysgalactiae) and to antimicrobial susceptibility (penicillin, gentamicin, cloxacillin, AMC).
The network made two things visible that ordinary statistics missed:

Concrete or rubber floors, hand stripping after machine milking, dry-cow therapy, and routine milking-machine cleaning were the four strongest levers for reducing Streptococcus spp. — the dominant pathogen.
Most isolates were resistant to penicillin G (40 %), but susceptible to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (81 %) and cloxacillin (64 %) — useful, concrete guidance for farmers’ first-line treatment.



Original schematic summarising the Bayesian network in Horpiencharoen et al. (2019): farm-management practices (slate-blue) → milk pathogens (ivory) → clinical signs (sage) and antimicrobial susceptibility (taupe). Redrawn by the author for this site. Source: Preventive Veterinary Medicine 164, 49–55 (DOI 10.1016/j.prevetmed.2019.01.014).

Read the paper → DOI 10.1016/j.prevetmed.2019.01.014

title: Pangolins, pathogens, and the price of land-use change
text: Welcome — thanks for stopping by. I wanted the first post here to be about something I keep thinking about as a vet, a wildlife disease ecologist, and someone who grew up in Southeast Asia: the places where people, wild animals, and pathogens are pushed closer together, and how often that push is something we do to ourselves.

title: Pangolins, pathogens, and the price of land-use change
text:
The pangolin on the cover
The most-trafficked wild mammal on Earth is almost certainly a pangolin. All eight species — four in Africa, four in Asia, including the Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) across the region I come from — are listed on CITES Appendix I, and all eight are in some shade of red on the IUCN list. Their scales, made of the same keratin as my fingernails, are smuggled by the tonne into traditional-medicine markets. Their meat is a luxury dish. Estimates from seizure data suggest more than a million pangolins have been pulled out of the wild over the last two decades, and every estimate people bother to make turns out to be an undercount.
That number matters beyond the animals themselves. Pangolins became household names in 2020 when their role in the early SARS-CoV-2 investigation put them briefly on every front page. I don’t think pangolins caused that pandemic. But the episode made something visible that wildlife veterinarians had been quietly writing about for years: illegally traded wildlife is a moving buffet of pathogens, carried through live-animal markets, back-road holding pens, airport baggage, and courier networks that no diagnostic lab has standing access to.

title: Pangolins, pathogens, and the price of land-use change
text:
Tracking wildlife in Southeast Asia
Part of why this is so hard to manage is that we have a very uneven picture of what’s moving around. My own work has been on the resident side of that picture — GPS collars on gaur and banteng, habitat-suitability models across thirteen Asian countries, stochastic disease models that ask what happens if a cattle-borne pathogen actually meets a wild bovid population.
A couple of things you learn quickly from that kind of tracking work:

Wild bovid habitat in Southeast Asia is fragmented and squeezed up against the working landscape. Over half of the habitat that is still ecologically suitable for gaur, banteng, and wild water buffalo sits outside protected areas. That isn’t a failure of conservation; it’s a description of a continent where national parks are islands in a sea of agriculture, plantation, and human settlement.
Where wild bovid habitat and domestic cattle density overlap, you get interface zones — forest edges, cropland borders, shared water points — that are exactly the kinds of places where pathogens like foot-and-mouth disease, haemorrhagic septicaemia, or brucellosis can move in either direction.
Illegal hunting, snaring, and wildlife trafficking cut right through these same zones. So the same corridors that matter for conservation are also the corridors that matter for pathogen movement and for the wildlife trade.

It is, in other words, one landscape with several problems stacked on top of each other.

title: Pangolins, pathogens, and the price of land-use change
section: Land-use change is a disease driver
text:
Land-use change is a disease driver
Most of the big emerging infectious disease events of the last fifty years — Nipah, SARS, MERS, Ebola, highly pathogenic avian influenza, monkeypox/mpox, SARS-CoV-2 — share a pattern. A pathogen that was quietly circulating in a wild host encountered humans (or human-adjacent animals like pigs, poultry, civets, or camels) because the edge between wild and not-wild shifted. A forest was cleared, a plantation was expanded, a cave was mined, a live-animal market scaled up, a trade route opened.
The published evidence on this has become hard to argue with. Ecological studies show that deforestation and landscape fragmentation correlate with increases in zoonotic disease spillover events, because they change which animals live where, which pathogens they carry, and how often any of that touches a human community. The wildlife trade amplifies the effect — it takes that edge and moves it, physically, into airports and cities.
The implication for my field is uncomfortable and, I think, freeing: surveillance designed around known pathogens and known hosts will always be chasing the last outbreak. Surveillance designed around the interfaces — forest edges being cleared, markets that handle wild species, transport chains that aggregate animals — has a chance of catching the next one.

title: Pangolins, pathogens, and the price of land-use change
text:
One Health, honestly
“One Health” gets used so often in grant applications that it can start to sound like a polite slogan. I want to try to keep it concrete on this blog. For me, One Health means at least three things:

Shared data and shared surveillance. Human, animal, and environmental health agencies in most of Southeast Asia (and most of the world) still track their own subsets of the picture in their own systems. The useful work is often the boring work of getting those datasets to speak to each other.
Conservation as disease prevention. Keeping forests standing, keeping wild populations viable, and enforcing wildlife-trade regulations aren’t separate from pandemic preparedness — they are pandemic preparedness, delivered upstream. The pangolin that stays in the forest doesn’t enter a supply chain.
Field-first, lab-second. The most important questions are almost never answered by a sample alone. They’re answered by someone who has actually stood in the farm, the forest edge, or the market, and can tell you what “normal” looks like there.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
This is a from-scratch guide assuming you’ve never used Quarto + GitHub Pages together. Plan to set aside ~45 minutes the first time. After that, updating the site is a one-command affair.
The steps are:

Install Quarto
Install Git & set it up
Preview the site locally
Add your photo and CV
Make the GitHub repo public
Connect this folder to your GitHub repo
Publish the site
Turn on GitHub Pages
Day-to-day: updating the site




Quarto is what turns your .qmd files into a website.

Go to https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/.
Download the installer for your operating system (Mac / Windows / Linux).
Run the installer. Accept the defaults.
Open a Terminal (Mac) or Command Prompt / PowerShell (Windows) and check it installed:
quarto --version
You should see a version number like 1.5.57. If you see “command not found”, restart your computer and try again — sometimes the new program needs that.


RStudio users: if you use RStudio 2022.07 or newer, Quarto is already bundled. But installing Quarto separately is still recommended so you can use it from the terminal.




Git is the version-control tool GitHub uses.

Go to https://git-scm.com/downloads and install Git for your OS.
In a terminal, set your name and email — GitHub uses these to label your commits:
git config --global user.name "Wantida"
git config --global user.email "wantidah@gmail.com"
Tell Git to use a branch called main (modern default):
git config --global init.defaultBranch main


Already have RStudio? You can do most of this in RStudio’s Git tab instead of the terminal. But the terminal is a one-time cost that pays off — all tutorials online use it.




Before publishing, let’s make sure the site builds on your computer.

Open a terminal.
Change into the website folder. If the folder lives on your Desktop, for example:
cd ~/Desktop/wantidah-website
(On Windows: cd %USERPROFILE%\Desktop\wantidah-website)
Start the preview server:
quarto preview
This will:

Build the site
Open your browser at something like http://localhost:4444
Watch your files — any time you save a .qmd file, it reloads

Click through the site. You should see the home page, About, Research, Publications, Blog, and Contact.
When you’re done, press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the preview.


⚠️ If you see errors, read them carefully. Usually it’s a typo in a .qmd front matter block (the bit between --- lines at the top).




Two assets that make a big difference:

Profile photo — save a square-ish photo as images/profile.jpg. About 800×800px is plenty. A warm, outdoorsy shot fits the site’s feel.
CV PDF — save as files/wantida-cv.pdf. The About page already links to this filename.

(Optional: a images/favicon.png — a small 32×32 or 64×64 icon that shows up in browser tabs.)
After adding these, quarto preview will pick them up automatically — no code changes needed.



GitHub Pages publishes from public repos on the free plan.

Go to https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io.
Click Settings (top of the repo page).
Scroll to the very bottom → Danger Zone.
Click Change repository visibility → Change to public.
Confirm by typing the repo name.


This is safe and standard for personal academic sites. Your repo name and your website content are already visible when the site is live.




Think of this as telling your website folder “hey, you’re the source for that GitHub repo.”

In your terminal, make sure you’re in the website folder:
cd ~/Desktop/wantidah-website
Initialize Git (creates a hidden .git folder that tracks changes):
git init
git branch -M main
Stage and commit all the starter files:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial site scaffold"
Connect to your GitHub repo:
git remote add origin https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io.git
Push your files up:
git push -u origin main
GitHub will ask you to sign in the first time. Use a Personal Access Token instead of your password — see https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens. Or, install the GitHub CLI and run gh auth login once — it handles this for you.


Existing repo has files already? If the GitHub repo you created isn’t empty (e.g., it has a README), pull those first:
git pull origin main --rebase --allow-unrelated-histories
…then re-run git push -u origin main.




Quarto has a one-liner for publishing to GitHub Pages:
quarto publish gh-pages
The first time, it will:

Ask if you want to confirm publishing — type y.
Build the site.
Create a special Git branch called gh-pages in your repo that holds the rendered HTML (not your source files).
Push it.

You’ll see a URL like https://wantidah.github.io at the end.

If quarto publish gh-pages fails with “repo not found” or a permissions error, run gh auth login once and re-try.




GitHub needs one setting tweaked to serve your site.

Go to https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io/settings/pages.
Under Build and deployment → Source, pick Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, pick gh-pages and folder / (root).
Click Save.
Wait ~1 minute. Refresh the page — you’ll see a green banner: Your site is live at https://wantidah.github.io.




Once the setup is done, the loop is short.
Edit locally:
quarto preview      # live preview as you edit
Publish changes:
# 1. Save your source to GitHub (your .qmd files)
git add .
git commit -m "Update publications list"
git push

# 2. Re-render & publish the rendered site
quarto publish gh-pages
Changes usually appear at https://wantidah.github.io within a minute.
Add a new blog post:
mkdir posts/2026-05-bats-and-ranches
Create posts/2026-05-bats-and-ranches/index.qmd:
---
title: "Bats and ranches: notes from the field"
description: "What we saw in northern Thailand this May"
date: "2026-05-02"
categories: [wildlife, field-notes, one-health]
image: thumbnail.jpg
---

Your post text goes here, in plain markdown.
Put a thumbnail.jpg in the same folder for the blog listing card. Preview, commit, push, publish.




“quarto: command not found” Quarto isn’t on your PATH. Restart your terminal / computer. On Mac, check which quarto. On Windows, re-run the installer and tick the “add to PATH” box.
Pages shows a README instead of the site The Pages source is pointing at main instead of gh-pages. Revisit Step 8.
Site builds locally but Pages shows the old version GitHub Pages caches for 1–10 minutes. Hard-refresh your browser (Ctrl+Shift+R / Cmd+Shift+R).
I broke something and want to start over Nothing you do locally affects the live site until you push. Worst case: delete the local folder, re-clone from GitHub:
git clone https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io.git




Once the site is live and you’re comfortable with the loop:

Add a custom domain (optional) — e.g., wantida.science. https://docs.github.com/en/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Quarto is what turns your .qmd files into a website.

Go to https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/.
Download the installer for your operating system (Mac / Windows / Linux).
Run the installer. Accept the defaults.
Open a Terminal (Mac) or Command Prompt / PowerShell (Windows) and check it installed:
quarto --version
You should see a version number like 1.5.57. If you see “command not found”, restart your computer and try again — sometimes the new program needs that.


RStudio users: if you use RStudio 2022.07 or newer, Quarto is already bundled. But installing Quarto separately is still recommended so you can use it from the terminal.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Git is the version-control tool GitHub uses.

Go to https://git-scm.com/downloads and install Git for your OS.
In a terminal, set your name and email — GitHub uses these to label your commits:
git config --global user.name "Wantida"
git config --global user.email "wantidah@gmail.com"
Tell Git to use a branch called main (modern default):
git config --global init.defaultBranch main


Already have RStudio? You can do most of this in RStudio’s Git tab instead of the terminal. But the terminal is a one-time cost that pays off — all tutorials online use it.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Before publishing, let’s make sure the site builds on your computer.

Open a terminal.
Change into the website folder. If the folder lives on your Desktop, for example:
cd ~/Desktop/wantidah-website
(On Windows: cd %USERPROFILE%\Desktop\wantidah-website)
Start the preview server:
quarto preview
This will:

Build the site
Open your browser at something like http://localhost:4444
Watch your files — any time you save a .qmd file, it reloads

Click through the site. You should see the home page, About, Research, Publications, Blog, and Contact.
When you’re done, press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the preview.


⚠️ If you see errors, read them carefully. Usually it’s a typo in a .qmd front matter block (the bit between --- lines at the top).

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Two assets that make a big difference:

Profile photo — save a square-ish photo as images/profile.jpg. About 800×800px is plenty. A warm, outdoorsy shot fits the site’s feel.
CV PDF — save as files/wantida-cv.pdf. The About page already links to this filename.

(Optional: a images/favicon.png — a small 32×32 or 64×64 icon that shows up in browser tabs.)
After adding these, quarto preview will pick them up automatically — no code changes needed.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
GitHub Pages publishes from public repos on the free plan.

Go to https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io.
Click Settings (top of the repo page).
Scroll to the very bottom → Danger Zone.
Click Change repository visibility → Change to public.
Confirm by typing the repo name.


This is safe and standard for personal academic sites. Your repo name and your website content are already visible when the site is live.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Think of this as telling your website folder “hey, you’re the source for that GitHub repo.”

In your terminal, make sure you’re in the website folder:
cd ~/Desktop/wantidah-website
Initialize Git (creates a hidden .git folder that tracks changes):
git init
git branch -M main
Stage and commit all the starter files:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial site scaffold"
Connect to your GitHub repo:
git remote add origin https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io.git
Push your files up:
git push -u origin main
GitHub will ask you to sign in the first time. Use a Personal Access Token instead of your password — see https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens. Or, install the GitHub CLI and run gh auth login once — it handles this for you.


Existing repo has files already? If the GitHub repo you created isn’t empty (e.g., it has a README), pull those first:
git pull origin main --rebase --allow-unrelated-histories
…then re-run git push -u origin main.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Quarto has a one-liner for publishing to GitHub Pages:
quarto publish gh-pages
The first time, it will:

Ask if you want to confirm publishing — type y.
Build the site.
Create a special Git branch called gh-pages in your repo that holds the rendered HTML (not your source files).
Push it.

You’ll see a URL like https://wantidah.github.io at the end.

If quarto publish gh-pages fails with “repo not found” or a permissions error, run gh auth login once and re-try.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
GitHub needs one setting tweaked to serve your site.

Go to https://github.com/Wantidah/wantidah.github.io/settings/pages.
Under Build and deployment → Source, pick Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, pick gh-pages and folder / (root).
Click Save.
Wait ~1 minute. Refresh the page — you’ll see a green banner: Your site is live at https://wantidah.github.io.

title: Step-by-step: get your website live on GitHub Pages
text:
Once the setup is done, the loop is short.
Edit locally:
quarto preview      # live preview as you edit
Publish changes:
# 1. Save your source to GitHub (your .qmd files)
git add .
git commit -m "Update publications list"
git push

# 2. Re-render & publish the rendered site
quarto publish gh-pages
Changes usually appear at https://wantidah.github.io within a minute.
Add a new blog post:
mkdir posts/2026-05-bats-and-ranches
Create posts/2026-05-bats-and-ranches/index.qmd:
---
title: "Bats and ranches: notes from the field"
description: "What we saw in northern Thailand this May"
date: "2026-05-02"
categories: [wildlife, field-notes, one-health]
image: thumbnail.jpg
---

Your post text goes here, in plain markdown.
Put a thumbnail.jpg in the same folder for the blog listing card. Preview, commit, push, publish.
